hints: Look at the shape of the curve first, the starting pH near 0, the ending pH near 14 and the very steep jump through pH 7.
Notice the equivalence point is at 10 cm3 of Q even though you started with 20 cm3 of P at the same concentration.
Use the mole balance at equivalence, moles of $H^+$ must equal moles of $OH^-$, to work out how many $H^+$ per acid and $OH^-$ per base are needed.
walkthrough:
**Identify the type of titration from pH**

The curve starts very acidic (pH about 0.5) and finishes very alkaline (pH about 14). The vertical section is long, from about pH 2 to pH 12, with equivalence at pH 7.

That is the classic signature of strong acid plus strong base:
$$\text{strong acid in flask + strong base from burette}$$

**Use the equivalence volume to find stoichiometry**

You start with $20 \text{ cm}^3$ of P. Equivalence needs only $10 \text{ cm}^3$ of Q. Concentrations are equal, call it $c$.

$$\text{moles P} = 20c \quad \text{and} \quad \text{moles Q at equivalence} = 10c$$

**Balance $H^+$ against $OH^-$**

Let acid P release $n_H$ moles of $H^+$ per mole, and base Q release $n_{OH}$ moles of $OH^-$ per mole. At neutralisation:
$$20c \times n_H = 10c \times n_{OH}$$
$$2n_H = n_{OH}$$
So the base must release twice as many hydroxide ions as the acid releases hydrogen ions. That means a monoprotic strong acid with a diprotic strong base.

**Match to the table**

$\text{HCl}$ is monoprotic strong acid ($n_H = 1$). $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ is diprotic strong base ($n_{OH} = 2$). This fits both the strong-strong shape and the 20 to 10 volume ratio.

options.A: Both $\text{HCl}$ and $\text{NaOH}$ are strong, so the curve shape is correct, but both are monoprotic with $n_H = 1$ and $n_{OH} = 1$. With equal concentrations, $20 \text{ cm}^3$ of acid would need $20 \text{ cm}^3$ of base, not $10 \text{ cm}^3$.
options.B: $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is a strong diprotic acid and $\text{NH}_3$ is a weak base. A strong acid with weak base would end at pH around 8 to 10, not 14, and have equivalence below pH 7. Stoichiometry is also wrong, it would need $40 \text{ cm}^3$ of $\text{NH}_3$.
options.C: $\text{HCl}$ is a strong monoprotic acid giving the very low starting pH, and $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ is a strong diprotic base giving the very high final pH and steep jump through pH 7. With $n_H = 1$ and $n_{OH} = 2$, $20 \text{ cm}^3$ of acid needs exactly $10 \text{ cm}^3$ of base at the same concentration.
options.D: $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ is a weak acid, so the starting pH would be about 3, not below 1. A weak acid with strong base also has equivalence above pH 7. Although $\text{Sr(OH)}_2$ is diprotic and gives the correct 10 cm3 volume, the curve shape rules this out.
